description:
▶ NEW VIDEO: What If You Were the Only Man on an Island of 100 Amazons? https://youtu.be/UtXsABU4Cek

You wake up tomorrow, open your closet... and there's nothing in it. Not even socks. In this world, humans never invented clothes.

So we walked through seven rooms of that world: the cold, the sun, the office, the awkward part, the missing industry, space... and the morning Kevin had an idea.

Would you survive one day in this world? Tell us in the comments.

Real facts in this video
• Clothing is roughly 170,000 years old: body lice, which live in clothes, split from head lice around then. Toups et al., Molecular Biology and Evolution 28(1), 2011. https://doi.org/10.1093/molbev/msq234
• Below about 27 °C a resting naked body has to spend extra energy to stay warm (estimates of this lower critical temperature run 27–30 °C): Speakman & Keijer, Molecular Metabolism 2(1), 2013. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.molmet.2012.10.002
• Earth's average temperature is about 15 °C: NASA Earth Fact Sheet. https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/earthfact.html
• Unprotected skin can be damaged by the sun in as little as 15 minutes: CDC, Sun Safety. https://www.cdc.gov/skin-cancer/sun-safety/
• More than 100 billion garments were made in 2014, nearly 14 for every person on Earth: McKinsey & Company, Style that's sustainable (2016). https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/sustainability/our-insights/style-thats-sustainable-a-new-fast-fashion-formula
• Richard Arkwright patented his water-powered spinning frame in 1769: Encyclopaedia Britannica. https://www.britannica.com/biography/Richard-Arkwright

Kevin, the squirrel and everyone else are fictional. Any resemblance to real Kevins is a coincidence.

title: Iran Buried the Doors. Now the US Wants to Bomb What's Inside.
description:
Since 2020, Iran has been digging a tunnel complex into Kuh-e Kolang Gaz La, "Pickaxe Mountain", about 2 km south of the Natanz enrichment site. Since August, two of its four entrances have been packed with earth and the roads to the other two blocked. UN inspectors have never been inside. And the US President has said on the record: "We're going to take out Pickaxe Mountain."

The problem: America's biggest bunker buster, the 30,000-pound GBU-57, is publicly rated to dig about 60 meters (200 feet). Analysts estimate the facility sits at least 100 meters down.

This file rebuilds the mountain in 3D from real elevation data, follows the dig in Sentinel-2 satellite images from 2018 to 2026, and walks through what may be inside and every option for reaching it: the air vents, sealing the doors, the MOAB, a bomb that isn't finished yet, and the oldest option of all.

CHAPTERS

00:50 Exhibit A: The target
02:20 Exhibit B: The dig
03:38 Exhibit C: The depth
04:57 Exhibit D: The bomb
06:29 Exhibit E: The options

The tunnel interiors are illustrations, because the real layout is not public. Strike sequences are labeled simulations.

title: The Deadliest Booby Traps of the Vietnam War
description:
In this video we go deep into the booby traps used by the Viet Cong against American and South Vietnamese soldiers: punji stick pits smeared with filth, the Venus Flytrap, the swinging mace, the cartridge trap, the bamboo whip, and grenades rigged with tripwires inside tin cans. Cheap to build, almost impossible to spot, and designed not always to kill, but to maim, slow down entire units and break the nerve of men who had to walk point every single day.

Then we go underground. Beneath Cu Chi ran hundreds of kilometers of tunnels, and the men sent down there were the Tunnel Rats: small, volunteer soldiers armed with a pistol, a knife and a flashlight, crawling through pitch-black passages full of trapdoors, spikes, snakes and enemy fighters waiting in the dark. Few jobs in the entire war were more terrifying.

We’ll look at how each trap worked, why they were so effective in guerrilla warfare, what US soldiers did to survive them, and the psychological toll they left on the GIs who came home.

If you’re into dark history, military history and the brutal side of war that rarely makes it into the textbooks, you’re in the right place.
